scenes.heading: DNA technologies and ethics
scenes.sub: How a single hair can solve a crime
scenes.say: Scientists can now copy a tiny amount of DNA millions of times, sort it by size and compare it between people. That helps solve crimes and diagnose conditions, but it also raises big questions about privacy.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A photocopier where every copy is copied again: 1, 2, 4, 8
scenes.science: PCR doubles a chosen section of DNA every cycle
scenes.breaks: a photocopier copies the whole page; PCR copies only the section between the primers, and copying slows as supplies run out.
scenes.say: PCR, the polymerase chain reaction, is like a photocopier where every copy gets copied too. The pile doubles each cycle: one, two, four, eight. Primers mark where the section starts and ends, and a heat-stable DNA polymerase does the copying.

scenes.heading: PCR: hot, cool, warm
scenes.say: Each cycle has three steps. Remember: Don't Annoy Elephants. Denaturation at about ninety-five degrees separates the strands. Annealing at about fifty to sixty-five degrees lets primers stick. Extension at about seventy-two degrees builds new strands.
scenes.caption: Each cycle has three steps. Remember: Don't Annoy Elephants. Denaturation at about 95 °C separates the strands. Annealing at about 50–65 °C lets primers stick. Extension at about 72 °C builds new strands.

scenes.heading: PCR doubles every cycle
scenes.say: Starting from one copy, the number of copies is two to the power of the number of cycles. Ten cycles gives one thousand and twenty-four. Thirty cycles gives over a billion.
scenes.caption: Starting from one copy, copies = 2ⁿ, where n is the number of cycles. 10 cycles gives 1,024. 30 cycles gives over a billion.

scenes.heading: Gel electrophoresis
points: DNA is negative: moves to the + electrode
A DNA ladder gives known sizes
scenes.say: Gel electrophoresis sorts DNA by size. DNA is negatively charged, so it moves towards the positive electrode. Like small kids weaving through a crowd, smaller fragments move faster and further. A DNA ladder of known sizes lets you compare.

scenes.heading: Paternity case
scenes.question: At one STR: Mother 120, 150. Child 150, 180. Man 1: 130, 160. Man 2: 180, 200. Who could be the father?
lines: So 180 must come from the father
scenes.say: DNA profiles compare short tandem repeats, or STRs. A child gets one band from each parent. Here, the child's one-fifty band matches the mother, so the one-eighty band came from the father. Only Man two has it. Real cases check many STRs.
scenes.caption: DNA profiles compare short tandem repeats (STRs). A child gets one band from each parent. Here, the child's 150 band matches the mother, so the 180 band came from the father. Only Man two has it. Real cases check many STRs.

scenes.heading: Please Consider Different People
points: Privacy: who can see your DNA?
scenes.say: DNA technologies raise ethical questions. Remember: Please Consider Different People. Privacy, consent, discrimination, and the people affected, including relatives who never agreed to testing. There's often no single right answer.

points: Child's bands match mum or dad
scenes.say: Quick recap. PCR copies DNA in cycles that double each time. Gels sort DNA by size, with small fragments travelling furthest. Profiles compare STRs, and the ethics matter too. Now try the practice questions!
